facts.statement: The genus Arechia was described by Cappetta in 1983.
Arechia inhabited the northern Tethys Ocean during the Early Eocene.
facts.quote: It is known from two species (one known from articulated remains, the other from isolated teeth) that inhabited the northern Tethys Ocean during the Early Eocene.

facts.statement: Isolated teeth of Arechia have been found potentially as late as the Early Oligocene.
facts.quote: Isolated teeth of this genus are also known, potentially as late as the Early Oligocene.

facts.statement: Arechia is considered the oldest known genus of stingaree.
facts.quote: It is the oldest known stingaree genus

facts.statement: The species A. arambourgi was named for Camille Arambourg, who originally classified the teeth as Raja praealba in 1952.
facts.quote: It is named for Camille Arambourg, who originally ascribed these teeth to Raja praealba in 1952.

facts.statement: Henri Cappetta erected the genus Arechia in 1983, separating males originally called A. arambourgi from females placed in Merabatis.
facts.quote: Henri Cappetta revised the species in 1983, erecting this genus for those Arambourg called males in this genus and placed the ones he called females in Merabatis.

facts.statement: The environment where A. crassicaudata lived matches the typical warm, shallow habitat of modern stingarees.
facts.quote: The inferred environment of the Monte Postale site where this species is found matches with the typical warm, shallow environment of extant representatives of this family.

facts.statement: Isolated teeth of Arechia are known from sites in Senegal, Tunisia, and potentially Egypt.
facts.quote: In addition to these two species, isolated teeth of Arechia sp. are known from several sites throughout North Africa, including from the Ypresian & Lutetian of Senegal, Bartonian of Tunisia, and potentially the Rupelian of Egypt.

facts.statement: Arechia lived between 59.24 and 37.71 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Thanetian to Bartonian (59.24 to 37.71 million years ago)
